title: WXIII: Patlabor the Movie 3
full_review:
The animated "WXIII: Patlabor The Movie 3" (Pioneer) is a confusing story, although less so for those familiar with the prolific Japanese video, comic book and TV and movie series.

For the uninitiated, it helps to have thick press notes with a glossary that gives name to the ravenous, biological monster-machine, WXIII, that two police detectives eventually discover is the cause of mysterious deaths around the Tokyo waterfront. "Labors" are industrial giant robots operated by humans, while Patlabor refers to the Tokyo Police Department's own patrol robots dealing with Labor-related crimes.

Director Takayama Fumihiko's animation is sometimes exceptional in its use of perspective and the characters' facial expressions can be quite evocative. Particular attention has been paid to the sound effects as well.

Yet the movie becomes a mishmash of sci-fi Japanese monster movie, murky conspiracy thriller and plodding police procedural. It's a long haul to the climax despite the unexpected thread of tragedy developed in the last half-hour.

Called in to investigate a series of deadly accidents around Tokyo Bay, laconic Senior Detective Kusumi (voice of Katsuhiko Watabiki) prefers old-fashioned personal questioning of witnesses while his younger partner, Hata (voice of Hiroaki Hirata), is a whiz on computer tracking of individuals and corporations that may be involved. Suspicion falls on a biomedical laboratory, and Hata is disturbed to find his new girlfriend, Saeko (voice of Atsuko Tanaka), is a genetic research scientist there.

In a frighteningly filmed close encounter, the two cops discover the waterfront killer is a huge biological organism-weapon whose origins trace right back to Saeko's lab.

Dropped into the mix is suspicion of an American military conspiracy, and the sole character to speak English lets loose a totally gratuitous stream of rough language. After Hata learns why Saeko was intimately involved in the secret creation of WXIII, the monster is lured from the depths of Tokyo Bay (shades of Godzilla?) to face down the police department's sturdy Patlabors.

The director deserves credit for developing the human relationships among Hata, his partner and his girlfriend rather than just focusing on robots and the humongous monster machine in their midst. But the blend of romance, action, mystery and sci-fi is jumbled and the pacing listless. In the end the film seems as awkward as its title.

Subtitles.

Because of some fantasy violence, a suicide and several instances of rough language, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
